title: Zyzz Was the Original Looksmaxxer. His Rise and Untimely Death Feel More Relevant Than Ever
gist: A new documentary, Poster Boy: Becoming Zyzz (Apple TV and Prime Video, directed by Selina Miles), traces how Australian bodybuilder Aziz 'Zyzz' Shavershian pioneered the engagement-farming, supplement-selling playbook of today's manosphere creator economy before dying at 22 in 2011. The economics are the story: Zyzz earned roughly $20,000 in his final three months, while his successors now make millions from the same formula, which the director calls 'a gigantic pyramid scheme.'

insights.claim: Australian fitness influencer Aziz 'Zyzz' Shavershian reportedly earned about $20,000 in the final three months of his life in 2011 at the peak of his global fame, an amount the director of a documentary about him describes as a drop in the bucket relative to what major creators earn today.
insights.speaker: Miles Klee
insights.so_what: A concrete before/after benchmark for how much monetization infrastructure has been built around influencer audiences in 15 years — the audience existed in 2011, the payment rails and supplement funnels did not.
insights.quote: reportedly making about $20,000 in the last three months of his life, which would now be considered a drop in the bucket by major creators

insights.claim: Manosphere streamers and podcasters today can make millions selling supplements and courses to young men seeking self-improvement, a monetization stack the documentary's director characterizes as 'a gigantic pyramid scheme.'
insights.speaker: Miles Klee
insights.so_what: The male self-improvement funnel is now a material consumer-spending channel for supplement and info-product brands; the pyramid-scheme framing is the reputational and regulatory risk attached to it.
insights.quote: It makes you realize how much has changed, because you look at how it works today, and it's extraordinary, it's just a gigantic pyramid scheme

insights.claim: Zyzz created a Facebook page titled '10,000 likes and I'll bash Zyzz' to farm engagement from his own detractors, then renamed the page into a promotional channel for his protein brand once it had scale — an early demonstration of converting hostile attention directly into product distribution.
insights.speaker: Miles Klee
insights.so_what: The rage-bait-to-audience-to-supplement-brand pipeline is a repeatable, still-operating growth mechanic — useful for evaluating the durability of creator-led consumer brands whose CAC is negative-cost outrage.
insights.quote: When the page was doing well, he switched the name of it to be promotion for his protein brand.
insights.locator: While Zyzz promoted values of inclusion

insights.claim: Zyzz maintained fake social media accounts to amplify the conflict between himself and his critics, having understood earlier than most creators that controversy drives clicks.
insights.speaker: Miles Klee
insights.so_what: Manufactured-conflict engagement is a founding technique of the influencer economy, not a late degeneration — relevant to platform trust-and-safety spend and to due diligence on creator-brand audience quality.
insights.quote: He understood sooner than most how controversy drove clicks, and even maintained fake social accounts to amplify the war between himself and the haters.
insights.locator: While Zyzz promoted values of inclusion

themes.theme: Platform-era origins of the influencer template

insights.claim: Zyzz's rise happened when YouTube (launched 2005, when he was 16) and Facebook (available to him the following year) were not yet understood by almost anyone as routes to notoriety or income, making him a natural experiment in what the platforms' incentives produce absent a playbook.
insights.speaker: Miles Klee
insights.so_what: Frames the manosphere not as a recent political phenomenon but as an emergent product of 2005-2011 platform mechanics — implying platform design changes, not content moderation alone, are the lever.
insights.quote: At that moment, few imagined YouTube (launched in 2005, when he was 16) or Facebook (first available to him the following year) as a means to notoriety, let alone financial success.
insights.locator: Through a mixture of Zyzz's archival content

insights.claim: By 2010 Zyzz had accumulated more followers on Facebook than the sitting prime minister of Australia, an early demonstration that a single fitness creator could out-distribute a head of government on a social platform.
insights.speaker: Miles Klee
insights.so_what: A datable inflection point for creator-versus-institution attention share — the structural condition that later made influencer channels a primary political and commercial medium.
insights.quote: By then, we learn from the film, Zyzz had more followers on the platform than the prime minister of Australia at the time.
insights.locator: A 2010 post on his Facebook page

insights.claim: The documentary's director argues that algorithmic incentives actively corrupted a creator whose stated ideals were inclusion and mutual support, changing him as a person rather than merely amplifying a pre-existing persona.
insights.speaker: Miles Klee
insights.so_what: An incentive-design argument that shifts liability from individual creators toward platform recommendation systems — the framing that underpins ongoing platform-harm litigation and regulation.
insights.quote: the incentives of the algorithm “corrupted those, and changed him as a person,”
insights.locator: But Miles would like viewers to take different lessons

insights.claim: Zyzz's rhetoric turned homophobic, misogynist and contemptuous of anyone who had not optimized their physical form, including a 2010 Facebook post reading 'id rather be dead than normal.'
insights.speaker: Miles Klee
insights.so_what: Documents the ideological drift baked into optimization-culture content, the reputational tail risk brands take on when they sponsor the aesthetics/self-improvement niche.
insights.locator: His rhetoric turned homophobic and misogynist

themes.theme: Physical-optimization risk and the drug stack

insights.claim: Zyzz used steroids to build his physique, Xanax to manage the stress and paranoia of public recognition, and publicly bragged in a video about obtaining clenbuterol — a drug prescribed for asthma in horses that carries a likelihood of dangerous cardiovascular side effects in humans.
insights.speaker: Miles Klee
insights.so_what: The optimization-influencer category has an unpriced pharmacological liability layer; enforcement or platform bans on PED-adjacent content would hit the same creators who anchor supplement brand sales.
insights.quote: he bragged about obtaining clenbuterol, a prescription drug used to treat asthma in horses, prized by bodybuilders as a supposedly performance-enhancing substance
insights.locator: And while acolytes copied his basic workout routines

insights.claim: The documentary discloses for the first time that Zyzz's toxicology report attributed his 2011 death at age 22 to acute respiratory failure caused by a combination of morphine, cocaine and benzodiazepines, after Thai authorities also found he had purchased a wide variety of pharmaceutical drugs and undergone multiple facial surgeries there.
insights.speaker: Miles Klee
insights.so_what: A 15-year-old cause of death withheld from the public is the documentary's news hook — a reminder that medical-tourism and PED supply chains sit underneath a consumer category marketed as wellness.
insights.quote: acute respiratory failure brought on by a combination of morphine, cocaine, and benzodiazepines
insights.locator: The exact cause of Shavershian's death

themes.theme: Legacy brands and the contrarian read on male loneliness

insights.claim: Zyzz's brother Said 'Chestbrah' Shavershian runs a fitness brand that monetizes the legacy directly, selling T-shirts bearing both brothers' faces and the looksmaxxing slogan 'Mog Them All' — vocabulary that would have made little sense 15 years ago.
insights.speaker: Miles Klee
insights.so_what: Shows the estate-to-merch conversion pattern in creator culture and how fast subculture jargon becomes sellable product copy — a leading indicator for apparel and supplement branding.
insights.quote: sells T-shirts with illustrations of both of their faces and a zeitgeisty, looksmaxxing slogan that would have made little sense 15 years ago: “Mog Them All.”
insights.locator: Perhaps it was unavoidable that Zyzz would be mythologized

insights.claim: The documentary's director offers a contrarian read on the 'male loneliness epidemic' explanation for online radicalization, noting that Zyzz had a genuine and durable network of male friends who remain in touch today, and that it was he who isolated himself from them as they tried to help.
insights.speaker: Miles Klee
insights.so_what: If loneliness is the wrong diagnosis, the products and policy interventions built around 'connection' for young men are mistargeted — worth watching for anyone underwriting the men's-mental-health or community-app category.
insights.quote: “might not be the right term for what we're actually seeing.”

insights.claim: The film leaves open how far Zyzz served as a template for misogynist influencer Andrew Tate, while noting Zyzz did not preach from nihilism or cynicism and maintained a genuine community — a distinction between the original self-improvement formula and its later, harder-edged commercial derivatives.
insights.speaker: Miles Klee
insights.so_what: Separates the durable demand signal (young men wanting agency and hope) from the specific personalities monetizing it — the demand outlives any individual creator's legal or reputational collapse.
insights.locator: Poster Boy leaves it up to the viewer

insights.claim: Demand for the underlying message remains intact and arguably stronger, with the director stating that more than ever men are seeking the promise that they can master their own universe, control their fate and become who they want to be.
insights.speaker: Miles Klee
insights.so_what: A persistent, growing demand pool that supplement, fitness, coaching and streaming businesses will keep competing to capture regardless of platform crackdowns on individual figures.
insights.quote: More than ever, men are seeking that sense of hope.
insights.locator: Yet his formula has clearly endured
